(B) Single, rounded, and plaque-like erythematous lesion with regular edges in the soft palate. (C) In the soft palate and tonsil pillar, note an irregular and granular lesion with haemorrhagic dots. (D) On the ventral surface of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and lower alveolar ridge, note a granular, ulcerated and erythematous appearance with yellowish dots. (E) Moriform appearance with irregular and exophytic nodules in the right buccal mucosa. Note that the lesion extends to the vestibule, labial commissure, and vermilion of the lower lip. (F) In the lower alveolar ridge and retromolar trigone, note an erythematous and ulcerated granular lesion with yellowish dots.

In 40 cases, one (42.1%) anatomical site was affected, followed by 32 cases affected at two (33.7%) sites, 12 (12.6%) at three sites, and 11 (11.6%) at four or more sites. The gingiva/alveolar ridge (n=40/23.4%) was the most commonly affected site, followed by lip/labial commissure (n=33/9.3%), and buccal mucosa (n=27/15.8%). plate_findings.evidence: gingival and lingual frenulus “mulberry-like” ulcers with hemorrhagic dots
cervical inflammatory lymphadenopathy

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A shows gingival oral ulceration described as mulberry-like with hemorrhagic dots, textbook moriform stomatitis of chronic PCM in PCM review article. B: Panel B shows tongue ulcer with hemorrhagic dots described in chronic PCM, consistent with moriform stomatitis manifestation. C: Panel C shows nodular/papular/ulcerated skin lesions and cervical swelling attributed to acute/subacute PCM; cervical lymphadenopathy is in vocabulary and visible swelling supports it, skin polymorphism captured as proposed findings. D: Panel D shows disseminated PCM in PCM-HIV co-infection with cervical lymphadenopathy plus widespread ulcerated crusted lesions and thoracoabdominal abscesses; lymphadenopathy maps to vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Peçanha et al. Paracoccidioidomycosis: What We Know and What Is New in Epidemiology, Diagnosis, and Treatment.. Journal of fungi (Basel, Switzerland) 2022. doi:10.3390/jof8101098. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Chronic form: gingival and lingual frenulus “mulberry-like” ulcers with hemorrhagic dots; (B) chronic form: deep ulcerative lesion on the tongue with infiltrative borders, hemorrhagic dots, covered with fibrin; (C) acute/subacute form: multiple polymorphic (nodular, papular, and ulcerated) skin lesions and cervical inflammatory lymphadenopathy; (D) disseminated form in a patient with PCM and HIV co-infection; the following may be seen: cervical lymphadenopathy, exuberant ulcerated, crusted skin lesions, and larges subcutaneous abscesses in the thorax and abdomen.
in_text_mentions: 53]. The main manifestation of chronic PCM in approximately 90% of patients is pulmonary, with symptoms of cough, dyspnea, and sputum expectoration [3,41]. A recent study by Dutra et al. [62] in a southeastern Brazilian hospital found that 59.6% of the patients with PCM had granulomatous ulcerated oral lesions. The oral lesions (Figure 2A,B) may be the first visible physical manifestation of the disease noticed by the patient, and may lead to a prompt diagnosis. However, even with adequate treatment, patients may develop the residual form of PCM, owing to fibrosis of the affected organs [3,5].

The acute/subacute form of the disease shows rapid and disseminated progression in the form of skin lesions; lymphadenopathy; and eventual suppuration, fever, and anorexia (Figure 2C) [3,41,63]. This form characteristically develops a few weeks or months after fungal exposure [2].

ical form of PCM, with characteristics of both chronic and acute forms of the disease, has been observed. Pulmonary involvement can coincide with generalized adeno- and hepatosplenomegaly. In patients with the mixed form, multiple, exuberant skin involvement; lytic bone lesions; and central nervous system involvement can be present, indicative of severe disease (Figure 2D). Patients with HIV co-infected with PCM make up the bulk of immunosuppressed patients with PCM; however, cases of PCM in transplant patients and those receiving immunobiological therapy have also been reported [63,64,65,66].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial non-contrast CT from paracoccidioidomycosis review showing asymmetric adrenal thickening/enlargement with calcification, described in caption and in-text as acute enlargement and chronic calcification phase of adrenal paracoccidioidomycosis. B: Coronal post-contrast CT same patient as A showing asymmetric adrenal thickening/enlargement, attributed to paracoccidioidomycosis by caption and article context. C: Axial post-contrast CT of second patient showing adrenal thickening in paracoccidioidomycosis review figure; in-text states adrenal is most commonly affected abdominal organ with diffuse enlargements. D: Coronal post-contrast CT of second patient showing adrenal thickening in paracoccidioidomycosis review figure; consistent with described adrenal involvement.

in_text_mentions: ily involve the adrenal glands, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and intestinal loops. The adrenal gland is the most commonly affected abdominal organ. There may be diffuse enlargements of the gland with heterogeneous attenuation on CT and MRI, with peripheral contrast enhancement in the acute form of the disease. Adrenal atrophy and calcification are usually observed during the chronic phase (Figure 6). Differential diagnoses should include other granulomatous infections, such as histoplasmosis and tuberculosis; old hemorrhage; and neoplasms, such as lymphoma, primary tumors, and metastases [131].

panels.figure_caption: Clinical aspects of oral paracoccidioidomycosis. (A) Mulberry-like ulcers with hemorrhagic dots in the anterior lower gingiva. Poor oral hygiene and associated severe periodontitis are observed. (B) Multiple granular, erythematous, and ulcerated lesions involving the upper alveolar ridge, labial vestibule, and mid-dorsal region of the tongue. (C) Crusted, ulcerated nodule with indurated borders located in the transition between the vermilion of the lip and the outer edge of the lower lip. (D) Moriform appearance and hemorrhagic dots in the anterior lower gingival region. The granular appearance is also seen in both the vestibule and labial mucosa. (E) Irregular, indurated, granular lesion involving the labial commissure and vermilion of the lower lip, as well as the adjacent skin. Note that the lip contour is lost. (F) Diffuse reddish lesion with classic Mulberry-like appearance involving the ventral surface of the tongue. (G) In the border of the tongue, note a yellowish ulcer with ill-defined contours. (H) Exuberant, ulcerated, reddish-white granular lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. The rolled anteroposterior margin was indurated on palpation.

(B) Multiple granular, erythematous, and ulcerated lesions involving the upper alveolar ridge, labial vestibule, and mid-dorsal region of the tongue. (C) Crusted, ulcerated nodule with indurated borders located in the transition between the vermilion of the lip and the outer edge of the lower lip. (D) Moriform appearance and hemorrhagic dots in the anterior lower gingival region. The granular appearance is also seen in both the vestibule and labial mucosa. (E) Irregular, indurated, granular lesion involving the labial commissure and vermilion of the lower lip, as well as the adjacent skin. Note that the lip contour is lost. (F) Diffuse reddish lesion with classic Mulberry-like appearance involving the ventral surface of the tongue. (G) In the border of the tongue, note a yellowish ulcer with ill-defined contours. (H) Exuberant, ulcerated, reddish-white granular lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. The rolled anteroposterior margin was indurated on palpation.

in_text_mentions: ns observed on the chest radiograph of PCM patients with active disease can be classified as alveolar, interstitial, and mixed. The active alveolar lesions are consolidations simulating snowflakes (Figures 2F and 2G). The interstitial lesions can be reticular, characterized by thin linear opacities (Figures 2D and 4C); nodular, characterized by small (< 1.0 cm in diameter) nodules; or reticulonodular (Figure 4E), when both types of lesions are associated. The mixed lesions present both alveolar and interstitial opacities (Figures 2F and 3A), with predominance of one of them at times. In additi

Patients with active PCM present consolidation, ground-glass opacities, or interstitial lesions (Figures 2G, 3B and 2E), involvement of the axial interstitium, with wall-thickened bronchi and centrilobular nodules sometimes with tree-in-bud pattern, and involvement of peripheral interstitium with interlobular septa thickening (Figures 4D, 5A, 2G). Greater nodules and/or masses, with or without cavitation, and bronchiectasis can be observed (Figures 2A, 2B, 2C, 3B, 3C, 5C); however, pleural effusion is rarely observed.

: relapse, with active disease; clinical manifestations of pulmonary sequelae; and other disease, such as influenza or pneumonia. In this situation, the differential diagnosis between active PCM and its residual form should be performed. On chest CT scan, the presence of ground-glass opacities does not help to differentiate active from residual lesions, because they appear in both stages. On the other hand, tree-in-bud lesions are diagnostic of active disease, meaning bronchial dissemination of the disease (Figure 2E), although this type of lesion is also observed in other infectious diseases.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A displays H&E histopathology with granulomatous inflammation and multiple round Paracoccidioides yeast cells in tissue. Although the caption describes a clinical photograph of facial lesions, the actual image is histopathology showing fungal yeast cells consistent with paracoccidioidomycosis. Disease attribution is supported by the panel-specific caption and the disease-focused article title. B: Panel B shows H&E histopathology of a compact granuloma with epithelioid and giant cells, with a fungal cell visible in the cytoplasm of a giant cell, exactly as described in the caption. This is a classic histopathological presentation of paracoccidioidomycosis.

Paraclinical tests revealed a high neutrophil count in the blood, and contrast-enhanced chest tomography showed total stenosis of the right main bronchus (Figure 1). Further investigations, including spirometry, bronchoscopy, and nasal mucosa biopsy, confirmed the presence of Paracoccidioides spp. (Figure 2 and 3). The patient was treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate, followed by a 6-month course of itraconazole. Follow-up assessments indicated satisfactory progress, with improved symptoms and no need for supplemental oxygen at the time of hospital discharge.

Caption and in-text explicitly attribute the massive cervical lymph node enlargement to hematogenous dissemination of Paracoccidioides sp. in a patient living with HIV/AIDS (group B, 54-year-old woman, IRIS context), and the in-text ties this presentation to Fig 3 and cure of PCM. The visibly enlarged cervical/submandibular lymph nodes match the classic scrofula-like presentation of paracoccidioidomycosis. Skin is adequately lit and appears light; no ethnicity is stated, so none is inferred.

panels.figure_caption: Bulky lymphadenopathy due to hematogenous dissemination of Paracoccidioides sp. in a patient living with HIV/AIDS. Patient from group B, 54 years old, presenting a massive enlargement of cervical lymph nodes in the context of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
in_text_mentions: Two patients of group B progressed with clinical signs compatible with IRIS: a 33 year-old man and a 54 year-old woman. Both had TCD4+ cell count below 200 cells/mm3 at the time of diagnosis (188 and 93 cells/mm3, respectively) and presented enlarged fistulized lymph nodes and fever associated with the increased TCD4+ cell count, 2 and 4 months after starting ART, respectively. Systemic corticosteroid was necessary for three months for the first patient with clinical improvement. Both patients evolved with cure of PCM. (Fig 3).

panels.figure_caption: (A): Patient with subacute disseminated form of paracoccidioidomycosis exhibiting multiple umbilicated skin-colored papules on the face. (B): Coronal multiplanar reformatted computed tomography of the anterior chest wall demonstrating the presence of multiple osteolytic lesions with cortical rupture of the sternal body, manubrium, and both clavicles. (C): A photomicrograph showing the thick birefringent cell wall of the fungus and the typical pattern of multiple budding around the mother cell, which is a characteristic feature of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis infection.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed the presence of umbilicated skin-colored papules on the face (Figure 1A), neck, and upper limbs. He tested negative in the sputum test for pulmonary tuberculosis and serological tests for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed lymph node enlargement and the presence of multiple osteolytic lesions on the sternum and both clavicles (Figure 1B). The pulmonary parenchyma was normal. It was diagnosed as disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis (PCM) based on the presence of osteolytic lesions, diffuse lymph node enlargement, and cutaneous lesions in an epidemiological setting.

However, the diagnosis of PCM was confirmed upon identification of P. brasiliensis in the sample obtained from the chest aspirate (Figure 1C). The patient was diagnosed with a severe juvenile subacute form of PCM. He was administered with liposomal amphotericin B and showed substantial clinical improvement, with weight gain and improvement in the cutaneous and osseous lesions.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A shows an extensive ulcer on the right shoulder in a patient with paracoccidioidomycosis, a typical cutaneous manifestation. The lesion type (ulcer) is not covered by the provided findings vocabulary, so it is listed as a proposed finding. B: Panel B shows a facial ulcero-crusted lesion surrounded by papules and erythema with eyelid edema in a paracoccidioidomycosis patient (also described with ocular involvement). Caption links this panel to the disease; findings are not represented in the supplied vocabulary. C: Panel C demonstrates markedly enlarged cervical lymph nodes in a paracoccidioidomycosis patient, matching the vocabulary term for cervical/submandibular lymphadenopathy; in-text mention supports lymph node involvement in this disease. D: Panel D shows enlarged cervical lymph nodes with cutaneous fistulization in a paracoccidioidomycosis patient; both cervical lymphadenopathy and draining lymphocutaneous fistula match...

panels.figure_caption: Paracoccidioidomycosis patients diagnosed at INI-Fiocruz between 2014 and 2019: (A) extensive ulcer on the right shoulder; (B) ulcero-crusted lesion in the frontal region surrounded by papules and erythema with eyelid edema; (C) enlarged lymph nodes in the cervical region; and (D) enlarged lymph nodes in the cervical region with some fistulization of the skin.
in_text_mentions: The main organs affected in group A were the lungs, the oral mucosa, and the skin, while in group B, there was a predominant involvement of lymph nodes, lungs, and skin (Figure 2A,B).

There was a statistically significant difference observed for lymph node involvement (Table 2). In group B, eight (7.5%) patients had large and/or confluent lymph nodes in the form of large tumors (Figure 2C,D), reaching up to 6 cm in diameter, and one of them had an extrinsic compression of the biliary tract, requiring hospitalization and treatment with amphotericin B.

Two patients presented signs and symptoms suggestive of ocular involvement in the second period of the study (Figure 2B). The first, in addition to skin lesions on the face, presented with lymph node enlargement and weight loss and had dacryocystitis that resolved along with the other symptoms, requiring 24 months of treatment. The second presented with visual blurring concomitant with skin lesions and lymphadenopathy, and was ultimately cured, requiring 25 months of treatment.

in_text_mentions: Histological review of the mucosal lesions showed evidence of pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia and numerous microabscesses. In addition to well-organized and loose granulomas, the underlying lamina propria presented a diffuse inflammatory infiltrate with lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and multinucleated giant cells (Figures 1A, 1C, 1E).

Microabscesses were observed in 25 cases (64.1%). We observed that neutrophils were present in both microabscesses and loose granulomas, and absent in well-organized granulomas (Figures 1A, 1C, 1E). The statistical analysis revealed a greater quantity of fungi in cases with loose granulomas only when compared with those with loose plus well-organized granulomas (p = 0,0005, Chi-square test) (Table 2, Figure 2).

The immunohistochemical analysis showed positivity to Nrf2 in the nuclei of neutrophils (Figures 1B, 1D, 1F). The intensity was homogenous and strong in all cells containing positive nuclei. In 16 cases (48.4%), Nrf2 was present in the nuclei of the neutrophils of loose granulomas, thus highlighting them amongst the cells that participated in granuloma formation (Figure 1D). panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a human patient's right cervical/submandibular region showing two ulcerated lesions with erythematous borders and exudative/necrotic bases. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Coronal chest CT from the case of pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis (article title) showing ground-glass opacities with the reversed halo sign, a recognized but less common CT presentation of pulmonary PCM; human patient image, disease attribution strong. B: Axial chest CT from the same patient with pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis; ground-glass opacities with reversed halo sign, human patient image directly attributable to PCM. C: Magnified axial CT lung-window image showing ground-glass opacities and reversed halo sign in pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis; human patient image with explicit caption attribution. D: Histology/cytology of biopsied gingival lesion showing Paracoccidioides yeasts with double birefringent membranes and clustered spherical forms consistent with the classic multiple peripheral budding (mariner's wheel) pattern; cytological diagnosis confirmed P. brasiliensis.
panels.attribution_text: Queiroz et al. Pulmonary paracoccidioidomycosis showing reversed halo sign with nodular/coarse contour.. Radiologia brasileira 2016. doi:10.1590/0100-3984.2015.0071. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A,B,C: Computed tomography sections showing, principally, focal pulmonary ground glass opacities predominantly located in the middle fields, some of them either completely or partially surrounded by a thin and coarse consolidation ring representing the “reversed halo sign”. One can also observe some areas with subtle interlobular septa thickening. D: Histological slide of the biopsied gingival lesion demonstrating eosinophilic epithelial cells of the squamous and spinous layers; giant, “foreign-body” type cells containing isolated and clustered spherical fungi with double and birefringent membranes in association with inflammatory cells. The cytological diagnosis confirmed the presence of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.
in_text_mentions: Chest computed tomography (CT) in December 30, 2013 showed focal pulmonary ground glass opacities predominantly in the middle fields, some of them completely or partially surrounded by a thin and coarse consolidation ring representing the "reversed halo sign". Other findings include some areas with subtle interlobular septa thickening (Figures 1A, 1B and 1C).

Biopsy result: eosinophilic epithelial cells of the squamous and spinous layers, giant, "foreign-body" type cells containing isolated and clustered spherical fungi with double and birefringent membranes, in association with inflammatory cells. The cytological diagnosis confirmed the presence of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (Figure 1D).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Human cervical lymph node biopsy from the reported case of disseminated juvenile paracoccidioidomycosis. PAS-stained histopathology shows multiple outlined granulomas with intense neutrophilic (suppurative) inflammation and fungal structures, a classic histologic manifestation of Paracoccidioides infection; granulomas are circled on the image. Disease attribution is supported by the case-specific caption and disease-focused article title; age group and ethnicity are not stated in the caption or in-text mentions. [raw subtype: juvenile] B: Grocott's methenamine silver-stained section of the same human cervical lymph node biopsy shows the pathognomonic 'pilot wheel' (mariner's wheel) Paracoccidioides yeast with a central mother cell and radially arranged daughter buds, directly matching the vocabulary finding for multiple peripheral budding yeast cells. Disease attribution to paracoccidioidomycosis is unambiguous; no age or ethnicity is...

plate_findings.evidence: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis with multiple peripheral buds in the typical 'pilot wheel' configuration (arrow) (periodic acid-Schiff stain, 400×)
Birefringent rings, some of which show lateral budding cells being phagocytosed by multinucleated foreign-body giant cells (open arrow) (hematoxylin and eosin stain, 400×)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: PAS-stained histopathology from the patient's bone biopsy showing Paracoccidioides brasiliensis with the classic 'pilot wheel' multiple peripheral budding configuration; the in-text confirms the pathological study identified P. brasiliensis in this immunocompetent patient with osteomyelitis and pyoarthritis. B: H&E histopathology from the patient's biopsy showing Paracoccidioides cells being phagocytosed by multinucleated foreign-body giant cells, part of the granulomatous inflammatory response to the fungus; disease attribution is explicit in the caption and confirmed by the in-text pathological study. C: H&E histopathology from the patient's biopsy showing the chronic granulomatous inflammatory process with epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells surrounding the fungi, a hallmark tissue response in paracoccidioidomycosis; attribution is explicit in the caption and in-text.
panels.attribution_text: Michelan et al. Osteomyelitis and pyoarthritis resulting from local paracoccidioidomycosis in an immunocompetent patient: a case report.. Journal of medical case reports 2012. doi:10.1186/1752-1947-6-342. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Paracoccidioides brasiliensis with multiple peripheral buds in the typical ‘pilot wheel’ configuration (arrow) (periodic acid-Schiff stain, 400×); (B) Birefringent rings, some of which show lateral budding cells being phagocytosed by multinucleated foreign-body giant cells (open arrow) (hematoxylin and eosin stain, 400×); and (C) the chronic granulomatous inflammatory process characterized by epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells surrounding the fungi (hematoxylin and eosin stain, 100×).
in_text_mentions: arthritis drainage and a bone biopsy were performed and intravenous antibiotics were administered to our patient. The results of a pathological study confirmed the presence of P. brasiliensis (Figure 5) and fluconazole treatment was initiated (10mg/kg/day). Our patient is at the time of writing still undergoing treatment and showing significant improvements, confirmed by a reduction of laboratory markers of inflammatory/infection status: leukocyte count (10,000 to 6000; reference value <12,000); C-reactive protein (1.3 to 0.9mg/dL, reference value <0.6mg/dL), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate

in_text_mentions: ar microscopy and molecular testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative. Blood tests for cryptococcal antigen, syphilis, hepatitis A/B/C, and histoplasmosis were also negative. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) serology showed negative IgM, positive IgG, and a quantitative plasma DNA load of 297 IU/mL. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed right paratracheal lymphadenopathy, bilateral axillary chains, micronodular opacities, and bronchial thickening (Figure 2A and 2B). CT of the left lower limb demonstrated moderate joint effusion and anterior soft tissue edema, with preserved articular spaces.

Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy revealed chronic granulomatous dermatitis. Hematoxylin-eosin staining showed granulomatous inflammation, while Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining showed multiple budding yeast forms compatible with Paracoccidioides spp. (Figures 2C and 2D). Double agar gel immunodiffusion serology for PCM was positive at a titer of 1:16.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a case report titled "Adrenal Paracoccidioidomycosis." Arrows mark bilateral adrenal enlargement, predominantly right, matching the captioned manifestation and the vocabulary finding for enlarged adrenal glands. The in-text context confirms the adrenal biopsy showed Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (Grocott stain, steering-wheel budding yeast), so disease attribution to paracoccidioidomycosis is direct and specific. Adrenal involvement is a recognized less-common (variant) form rather than the classic mucocutaneous/pulmonary presentation. No age, ethnicity, or skin assessment is applicable or stated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E histopathology from a patient with skin ulcers and positive PCM serology; the caption describes chronic granulomatous ulcerated dermatitis with microabscesses, and the in-text states dermal granulomas on biopsy consistent with Paracoccidioides spp. (Figure 3). This is a real patient image showing the suppurative granulomatous inflammation typical of paracoccidioidomycosis. B: Grocott methenamine silver stain from the same patient's skin biopsy showing yeast-like fungal structures; the in-text explicitly attributes the Grocott-stained multiple budding fungal forms to Paracoccidioides spp. (Figure 3), confirming disease attribution for paracoccidioidomycosis. C: Oil-immersion Grocott image showing the pathognomonic 'mariner's wheel' / 'Mickey Mouse head' appearance of Paracidioides: a large mother yeast with multiple narrow-based budding daughter cells. The in-text confirms these Grocott-stained multiple budding forms are consistent...

in_text_mentions: A thorough physical examination revealed two skin ulcers with raised, well-defined borders on the chest and left arm (Figure 1). A dermatological consultation was requested, and direct examination of a smear of the skin lesions with 10% potassium hydroxide revealed yeast-like fungal structures. Histopathological analysis revealed dermal granulomas and fungal structures with multiple budding forms on Grocott staining consistent with Paracoccidioides spp. (Figure 3). Bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures were negative, whereas serological results for PCM were positive.

in_text_mentions: ctions such as aspergillosis, zygomycosis and fusariosis(31,32). In an attempt to narrow the differential diagnosis of diseases presenting with the reversed halo sign, findings of internal reticulation, peripheral halo thickness > 1.0 cm and pleural effusion favor the diagnosis of an angioinvasive fungal infection over that of organizing pneumonia, within the appropriate clinical context of immunosuppression(33,34). In group B, other infections were present in 33.3% of patients, including tuberculosis (25.0%), esophageal candidiasis (16.7%), and syphilis (8.3%).

panels.body_site: oral cavity (gingiva of the right maxilla)
panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a real human patient's mouth showing an erythematous, granular gingival lesion of the right maxilla with dental mobility. The caption describes the lesion, the article title focuses on paracoccidioidomycosis of the maxillofacial region, and the in-text report states biopsy confirmed PMC. The granular hemorrhagic gingival appearance is the classic oral presentation (moriform stomatitis) of paracoccidioidomycosis.

in_text_mentions: A 38-year-old male patient who was a rural worker and smoker presented to the clinic, and he denied comorbidities and complained about gingival bleeding when he brushed his teeth (Figure 11). Biopsy was performed since the lesion did not disappear after basic periodontal treatment. Pathologic examination revealed PMC; thus, antifungal therapy with Bactrim was initiated.

panels.body_site: oral mucosa (jugal mucosa, lips, buccal commissure)
panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of an open mouth showing ulcerated, granular, erythematous lesions with pinpoint hemorrhages in the buccal/jugal mucosa and lips, consistent with moriform stomatitis. The article title focuses on paracoccidioidomycosis in the maxillofacial region, and the in-text confirms PMC diagnosis by anatomopathology in this case. The presentation is the classic oral manifestation of paracoccidioidomycosis.

in_text_mentions: al hypertension attended the outpatient clinic complaining about “sore and pain in the lips and mouth.” Clinical examination revealed the presence of erythematous ulcers in the lips and oral mucosa; the patient had a slight limitation of mouth opening due to the inflammatory process installed in the lips (Figures 8 and 9). Diagnostic suspicion of malignant neoplasia or paracoccidioidomycosis was raised. After anatomopathological examination of multiple fragments collected under local anesthesia, PMC was confirmed. Antifungal therapy with Bactrim (trimethoprim + sulfamethoxazole) was conducted.

panels.figure_caption: A, Hepatic and multiple bone lesions in a 35-y-old female patient admitted with obstructive jaundice and ultimately diagnosed with the juvenile form of paracoccidioidomycosis. MIP (left) and axial fused PET/CT images (right) show multiple small focal lesions in the right clavicle, left scapula, both iliac bones, and the proximal left femur (thin arrows), none of which had been clinically detected. An infiltrative hepatic lesion is also observed (thick arrows). The MIP image additionally reveals involvement of cervical, mediastinal, axillary, and abdominal lymph nodes and physiological cardiac uptake. B, Pulmonary, adrenal, and testicular lesion (arrows) are seen in a 58-y-old man presenting with prolonged fever, cough, adrenal insufficiency, and Paracoccidioides sp. identified in sputum. Lesions are shown on MIP images (left) and fused PET/CT images (right).
in_text_mentions: Conventional evaluation classified 20 of 34 patients (59%) as multifocal—15 with only two foci—and 14 of 34 (41%) as unifocal. FDG-PET/CT reclassified 33 of 34 (97%) as multifocal—2 with two foci—with just 1 case (3%) unifocal (Figure 1). Overall, PET/CT detected 150 lesions compared with 62 by conventional methods (mean 4.4 ± 1.6 vs 1.8 ± 0.9 affected areas per patient). PET/CT identified additional lesions in lymph nodes, lungs, adrenal glands, bone, subcutaneous tissue, gastrointestinal tract, thyroid, and testes (Table 2, Figures 2 and 3).

panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemistry detection of chemokines and granule proteins in liver and lymph nodes from PCM patients. MBP (A,D), CCL5 (B,E) and CCL11 (C,F) were stained in cells distributed in inflammatory infiltrates of lymph nodes (LN) and liver from PCM patients (Original magnification x 400).
in_text_mentions: Liver and lymph nodes biopsies of patients with the acute/juvenile form of PCM were evaluated by immunohistochemistry in order to detect MBP, CCL5 and CCL11. Fig 1A and 1D show cells with morphology of eosinophils expressing MBP in the inflammatory infiltrate around fungal cells in the liver and lymph nodes, respectively.

CCL5 was detected in areas of hepatic parenchyma, as well as in giant cells (Fig 1B). In lymph nodes, CCL5 was mainly detected in giant cells, around P. brasiliensis yeast cells. CCL11-stained cells were diffusely demonstrated in the hepatic parenchyma (C) and lymph nodes (F). Altogether, the examined biopsies showed rich eosinophils infiltrates in close contact with fungal cells and MBP, an eosinophilic granule protein. In accordance, CCL5 and CCL11, chemokines involved in eosinophils recruitment, were also detected in P. brasiliensis infected tissues.

A: Sagittal T1 post-contrast MRI of the spinal cord in a 62-year-old man with confirmed paracoccidioidomycosis; in-text attributes the intramedullary nodular lesions at T10-T11 and L1 to PCM, and the article title ('Spinal cord and cutaneous involvement in paracoccidioidomycosis') supports spinal cord (CNS) involvement as a manifestation. No vocabulary finding covers spinal cord MRI, so the named imaging findings are placed in proposed_findings. Arrows annotate the enhancing lesions. Recognized but less common (CNS/spinal) form, hence variant; not skin, so skin_tone null; ethnicity not stated. B: Histology of a skin biopsy showing broad-based budding yeast cells; in-text explicitly states these confirmed paracoccidioidomycosis, and the article is on cutaneous/spinal PCM. This is the diagnostic (textbook) mycologic confirmation of PCM, hence classic. Arrow annotates the yeast. No skin tone assessable on a microscopy slide (null); ethnicity not...

panels.figure_caption: Sagittal T1 weighted images after contrast administration demonstrate intramedullary nodular enhancement at thoracic and lumbar levels (arrows) (A). Broad-based yeast cells (arrow) at histological samples (B).
in_text_mentions: A 62-year-old man, a gardener, was hospitalized in Southeast Brazil with a four-month history of weight loss, progressive lower limb paresthesia, muscle weakness, urinary and bowel incontinence, and skin lesions. On clinical examination, he had paraplegia and presented skin ulcers measuring two centimeters on the face and soles (Figure 1). Magnetic resonance imaging showed intramedullary nodular lesions at the thoracic (T10 -T11) and lumbar levels (L1) with peripheral enhancement (Figure 2A).

Identification of broad-based budding yeast cells on potassium hydroxide examination of cutaneous imprints confirmed paracoccidioidomycosis, which was also found in the microscopic analysis of a skin biopsy (Figure 2B). The patient was treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate during the in-hospital stay, and then released after being prescribed trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E histopathology of the right digit biopsy from a patient with paracoccidioidomycosis showing the classic large round yeast with multiple peripheral buds (mariner's wheel appearance), arrowed; article title and in-text confirm Paracoccidioides multiple budding. B: PAS-D histopathology of the same right digit biopsy showing budding yeast forms of Paracoccidioides in a paracoccidioidomycosis case; caption and in-text explicitly link the stain panel to the multiple-budding yeast finding. C: GMS stain of the right digit biopsy highlighting a large Paracoccidioides yeast with multiple peripheral buds (mariner's wheel), the classic diagnostic histologic appearance, in a case of paracoccidioidomycosis. D: GMS histopathology panel of the right digit biopsy showing the classic multiply-budding Paracoccidioides yeast (mariner's wheel / Mickey Mouse head pattern), arrowed, in a confirmed paracoccidioidomycosis case.

in_text_mentions: conducted to collect bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial lung biopsy (TBLB). PCR of the material was negative for tuberculosis, the direct test was negative for malignant cells, and fungi and culture showed no bacterial growth. TBLB material showed fungal structures compatible with cryptococcosis, blastomycosis, or PCM (not shown). We also observed concomitant disseminated painless, erythematous, rounded skin lesions with raised edges and central ulceration, and a skin biopsy was performed (Figure 2). The review of the BAL, TBLB, and skin biopsy contributed to the diagnosis of PCM.

Laboratorial analyses showed mild anemia (hemoglobin 9.4 mg/dL), worsening kidney function (previous creatinine 1.4, after 1.81 mg/dL), high inflammatory markers (c-reactive protein 10 mg/dL, ferritin 775 mg/dL), and low LDH levels (98 UI/mL). in_text_mentions: ospital, the patient was performed a right neck mass resection surgery. Postoperative pathological tissue examination indicated chronic granulomatous inflammation with a small abscess formation (Fig. 1A–C), suggesting a high risk of tuberculosis. Therefore, the doctor performed anti-tuberculosis treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin. One week later, drug-induced hepatitis occurred, and tuberculosis drugs were discontinued. Liver protection treatment was administered for 2 weeks, and the patient’s liver function improved. The patient’s right neck lymph nodes began t

When the patient was admitted, his vital signs were stable, consciousness was clear, and multiple swollen lymph nodes could be palpated on both sides of the neck. The right side was obviously enlarged, with the maximum mass of about 4.7 × 3.7 cm with a hard texture, tenderness, no wave sensation, no redness or swelling, and moderate mobility (Fig. 1D). The patient’s armpit and groin did not show any enlarged lymph nodes.

panels.rationale: Single frontal chest radiograph (side marker 'D' visible) of a real patient from an article disease-focused on paracoccidioidomycosis coinfection in PLHIV. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Frontal chest radiograph from the reported Chronic Multifocal Paracoccidomycosis case. The disease-focused article title, the caption, and the explicit in-text attribution of Fig. 3 to this PCM patient establish disease attribution; bilateral interstitial opacities at the lung bases are a classic pulmonary PCM manifestation. [raw subtype: chronic_multifocal] B: High-resolution chest CT (lung window) from the same reported Chronic Multifocal Paracoccidomycosis case; caption describes centrilobular and paraseptal emphysematous foci, a recognized chronic pulmonary sequela of PCM. The manifestation is not covered by the provided vocabulary, so it is recorded in proposed_findings; attribution rests on the case context and in-text link of Fig. 3 to the PCM patient. [raw subtype: chronic_multifocal]

plate_findings.evidence: intense granulomatous inflammatory process in the cecal appendix wall
Fungal structures and inflammatory infiltrate with multinucleated giant cells (400x, arrows indicating the fungal structures)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Low-power H&E section of the resected cecal appendix from a patient with paracoccidioidomycosis showing an intense granulomatous inflammatory process, a specific histopathologic manifestation of the target disease. B: High-power H&E of the cecal appendix showing multinucleated giant cells and arrows highlighting fungal structures, directly demonstrating Paracoccidioides sp. in a patient with paracoccidioidomycosis. C: Grocott-Gomori silver stain of the cecal appendix demonstrating numerous typical Paracoccidioides sp. yeast structures, confirming paracoccidioidomycosis in this resected patient tissue.
